phonemes.desc: Voiced alveolar trill [r], rolled with the tongue-tip as in modern Icelandic and Italian — never the English approximant.
Short close-mid front [e], held brief — the Old Norse short e, not a diphthong and not the long é.
Medial g after a vowel is the voiced velar fricative [ɣ] — a soft, breathy scrape in the throat, as in Spanish lago, never the hard stop of English go.
Short close front [i], unrounded and brief.
The long (geminate) nasal [nː], held audibly across the syllable boundary, as the manuscripts write it double.

pronunciation.approximation: 'REH-yin' is close — two beats, stress on the first, the medial g softened toward a light 'y'-like fricative ([ɣ], the g of Spanish lago), the final n held a fraction long.

kin.label: Old Norse
kin.form: Reginn, son of Hreiðmarr, foster-father of Sigurðr; the name is related to regin, 'the ruling powers, the gods' — the word that lives on in ragnarök, 'the doom of the regin'.

kin.label: Younger Futhark
kin.form: ᚱᛁᚴᛁᚾᚾ (r-i-k-i-n-n), the Viking-Age runic rendering, where ᚴ kaun writes both /k/ and /g/.

kin.label: Continental Germanic
kin.form: The cycle's Southern counterpart knows no Reginn by name; the Nibelungenlied's Mime (Old High German Mîme) is the corresponding smith-fosterer of Siegfried.

kin.label: Modern Scandinavian
kin.form: Regin, the simplified modern form — the doubled n collapsed and the soft fricative g hardened, as in modern Icelandic Reginn and Danish Regin.

pronunciation.note: Reginn is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: normalized Old Norse writes the name in six plain ASCII letters — no diacritic, no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The tier says something about orthography and nothing about the smith; only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input.

domains.title: Dwarf Smith, Fafnir's Brother
domains.subtitle: The Smith Who Forged a Dragon-Slayer
domains.lead: Reginn, son of Hreiðmarr and brother of Fáfnir and Ótr, is the master smith of the Völsung cycle — 'a dwarf in stature', the eddic prose says, 'wise, grim, and skilled in magic'. Cheated of his share of the cursed otter-ransom when his brother Fáfnir murdered their father for the gold, he fostered the young Sigurðr at King Hjálprek's court and reforged from the shards of Sigmundr's blade the sword Gram — the one weapon that could kill the dragon. But the hand that forged the slayer meant to claim the hoard, and when Sigurðr tasted the dragon's blood and understood the speech of birds, the foster-son turned Gram on the foster-father.

cards.name: The Sword Gram
cards.desc: Reforged from the shattered fragments of Sigmundr's blade — so keen it clove Reginn's anvil to the stock and cut a floating wool-pack in the Rhine against the current.

cards.name: The Anvil
cards.desc: The forge where Reginn's craft outran his loyalty: two blades broke there before Sigmundr's shards were brought, and the third stood the anvil's test.

cards.name: The Otter's Ransom
cards.desc: Andvari's gold and the ring Andvaranautr, paid to Hreiðmarr for Ótr's skin — the cursed hoard that set brother against brother and began the feud.

cards.name: The Nuthatches
cards.desc: The birds whose speech Sigurðr understood when Fáfnir's heart-blood touched his tongue: 'few would behave more wretchedly — cut off his head'.

symbols.name: The sword Gram
symbols.meaning: The reforged blade of Sigmundr's shards — craft completing a broken lineage, and the instrument of its maker's death

symbols.name: The anvil
symbols.meaning: The measure of true forging — two flawed blades broke on it before Gram stood the test

symbols.name: Andvaranautr
symbols.meaning: The cursed ring of the otter's ransom — the gold that killed Hreiðmarr, turned Fáfnir to a dragon, and armed Reginn's patience

symbols.name: The dragon's blood
symbols.meaning: The taste that opened bird-speech to Sigurðr — the moment the foster-son learned the foster-father's plan

symbols.name: The foster-bond
symbols.meaning: The tie Reginn made and meant to break — the deepest oath of the northern world, betrayed for a hoard

mythology.lead: Reginn's dossier runs through the whole Völsung cycle: the otter's ransom in Skáldskaparmál, the fosterage in Reginsmál and Völsunga saga, the reforging of Gram, and the death on Fáfnir's heath when the birds spoke. He is the cycle's great ambiguous figure — the finest smith in the tradition and its coldest traitor, teacher and would-be murderer of the same boy.

myths.title: The Otter's Ransom
myths.text:
It begins with a skinned otter. Óðinn, Hœnir and Loki came to Andvari's falls, where Reginn's brother Ótr fished in otter shape; Loki killed him with a stone, and that evening the gods carried the skin into Hreiðmarr's house and boasted of the catch. Hreiðmarr and his sons Fáfnir and Reginn seized the gods and demanded weregild: the otter's skin filled with gold, and covered with gold besides. Loki forced the dwarf Andvari to yield his hoard, and when Andvari tried to keep back one ring, Loki took that too — Andvaranautr. Andvari laid the curse: that gold would be the death of two brothers and the strife of eight princes, and no man should enjoy his wealth.

The curse kept its accounts. Hreiðmarr refused his sons any share of the ransom; Fáfnir killed his father in his sleep and took all the gold, and Reginn got nothing. Fáfnir went out to Gnitaheiðr, brooded on the hoard in the shape of a dragon, and Reginn — wronged, patient, and very clever — went to find an instrument.

myths.title: The Foster-Father
myths.text:
The eddic prose introduces him with exact economy: Reginn was Hreiðmarr's son, 'the most skilled of all men, and a dwarf in stature; he was wise, grim, and skilled in magic'. He came to the court of King Hjálprek in Denmark, where the boy Sigurðr — son of the slain Sigmundr and Hjördís — was being raised, and Reginn became his foster-father. The Völsunga saga lets him teach the boy chess, runes and tongues, and all the while he worked on the boy's pride: Fáfnir lies on Gnitaheiðr in dragon shape, he said, and your father left you nothing.

The foster-bond was the strongest tie the northern world knew short of blood — fosterage made family. Reginn made it in order to break it, and the tradition never forgives him for that inversion: every retelling keeps the same chill, that the hand which armed Sigurðr was already measuring him for the grave.

myths.title: The Reforging of Gram
myths.text:
Sigurðr demanded a sword, and Reginn forged him one — the best his craft could make. Sigurðr took it to the anvil and struck, and the blade shattered. Reginn forged a second, better than the first; it broke too. Then Sigurðr went to his mother and asked for the fragments of his father's sword — the blade Óðinn himself had shattered in Sigmundr's last battle — and Hjördís gave him the shards. From them Reginn reforged Gram: it shone in the forge, says the saga, like fire, and when Sigurðr struck the anvil the blade bit down to the stock and did not break. They laid a pack of wool on the Rhine, and the current carried it against the edge, and the sword cut it in two as easily as it cut water.

The scene is the tradition's purest statement about craft: Reginn's skill is real, peerless, and wholly in service of his revenge. He made the one weapon that could kill his brother — and put it into the hand of a boy he intended to outlive.

myths.title: The Blood on the Tongue
myths.text:
On Gnitaheiðr Sigurðr dug a pit in the dragon's path and drove Gram up into Fáfnir's heart from below. Dying, the dragon spent his last breath on a warning: Reginn betrayed me, and he will betray you. Reginn crept out, praised the killing, and asked one service — cut out the heart, roast it, and let me eat it. Sigurðr set the heart over the fire, and when he touched it to test the roasting and put his finger to his mouth, the dragon's blood touched his tongue and he understood the speech of birds. The nuthatches in the branches said: there sits Sigurðr roasting Fáfnir's heart — he should eat it himself and become wise; and Reginn lies in the heather, planning to betray the boy who trusts him; let the ring be the brother's ransom, and cut off his head.

Sigurðr took the counsel: he cut off Reginn's head, ate of the heart, and rode to the hoard. So the curse closed its second account — two brothers dead, Hreiðmarr and then Reginn, and the gold passed on with Andvaranautr, unspent and unenjoyed, exactly as the dwarf had sworn.

lore.syncretism: Reginn's clearest kin are inside the Germanic corpus itself. The Nibelungenlied's Mime — the smith who fosters Siegfried, forges for him, and schemes to send him against the dragon so the hoard will come free — is the Continental form of the same figure, softened in the High German epic but identical in structure: the fosterer who breeds his own instrument. Old English tradition preserves the smith-counterpart differently, in Weland the smith of Beowulf and Deor, the crippled artificer whose craft serves his revenge — the type to which Reginn belongs, the smith whose skill is inseparable from his grudge. Within the Norse corpus his brothers-in-craft are the dwarf-smiths of the gods: Brokkr and Sindri, who forge Mjölnir and Draupnir and Gullinbursti for stakes no higher than a wager — the clean contrast that shows what Reginn is, a smith whose work serves a feud instead of a boast. Nineteenth-century scholarship folded all of them into the type of the cunning artificer; the modern handbooks, Simek and Lindow among them, keep him where the sources put him: the Völsung cycle's necessary smith, indispensable and damned.
lore.culturalLegacy: Reginn's afterlife runs along two tracks. In the learned tradition he survived as part of the Völsung material — William Morris's Sigurd the Volsung (1876) gives the foster-smith his full cold arc, and Wagner compressed him with Mime into the Nibelung smith of the Ring cycle, where the brother-scheming-for-the-hoard survives almost intact. In the popular tradition the name lives quietly: Richard Wagner's Regin never recovered from Wagner's Mime, but Scandinavian legend and modern retellings of the Sigurðr story keep the foster-father and the reforged sword. Modern scholarship — Lindow, Byock, the Völsunga saga's commentators — treats him as the cycle's study in fosterage betrayed, the figure through whom the tradition asks what a teacher owes a student. He survives too in the comparative study of smith-legends, beside Weland and the Greek Hephaistos, as the northern proof that the master craftsman is never a safe ally.
lore.extendedMeditation: Reginn is the Edda's coldest lesson about skill without loyalty. Everything he makes is perfect: the teaching, the horse-choosing, the reforged blade, the patient plan. Everything he is fails. The tradition states the paradox without comment — the most skilled of all men, a dwarf in stature, wise and grim and versed in magic — and then lets the birds say what no human in the story can afford to say: the foster-father is lying in the heather, measuring the boy for a grave. What damns Reginn is not incompetence but inversion. Fosterage was the northern world's sacred adoption; the smith turned it into a tool. The sword he forged was true, and the hand that forged it was false, and the whole cycle hangs on the difference between those two sentences. In a mythology that runs on oaths, Reginn is the oath kept to the letter of revenge and broken in the spirit of kinship — and Gram, the blade that would not break, is the tradition's way of saying that craft outlives the craftsman, and testifies against him.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Reginn — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᚱᛁᚴᛁᚾᚾ (r-i-k-i-n-n), where ᛁ ís writes both /i/ and /e/ and ᚴ kaun writes both /k/ and /g/, so the transliteration rikinn is a normalized phonetic reconstruction. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: reginn.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Skáldskaparmál (the otter's ransom; Andvari's gold and Andvaranautr; the curse; Fáfnir's parricide and Reginn's exclusion), trans. Anthony Faulkes
Völsunga saga, chs. 13–20 (Reginn at Hjálprek's court; the fosterage; the reforging of Gram from Sigmundr's shards; the death of Fáfnir and of Reginn), trans. Jesse L. Byock

lore.archaeology: Reginn is a textual figure, but the Völsung cycle is among the most picture-rich narratives in the North, and the smith's scenes were carved. The great Sigurðr iconography of Viking-Age Scandinavia — the carving of the dragon-slaying, the heart-roasting, and the listening to birds — survives on the Swedish runestones at Ramsund (Sö 101) and Gök (Sö 327) in Södermanland, on the Drävle stone (U 1163) in Uppland, and on the Manx crosses at Jurby, Malew and Andreas, where the roasting scene and Sigurðr's thumb in his mouth are unmistakable. The Ramsund carving shows the full cycle's cast: the slain Fáfnir as a serpent-band, Sigurðr at the fire, the horse Grani loaded with the hoard, the birds in the tree — and the headless smith's tools laid beside a headless body, the standard scholarly reading of the truncated figure at the carving's edge as the killed Reginn. In England, the Halton cross in Lancashire and the York Minster grave slab carry related scenes. The manuscript witnesses are the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (Reginsmál, Fáfnismál), the codices of Snorri's Edda for Skáldskaparmál's prose account, and the vellum of Völsunga saga (AM 182 4to and the paper tradition) for the fullest prose life.
